records.name: Pakistan
records.current_summary:
Pakistan is dangerous — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act was "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition since 2009), but the Federal Shariat Court gutted it in 2023 (declaring provisions "un-Islamic"). Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi (bodies on a roadside), 267 violence cases were documented in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no Sharia cross-dressing criminalisation (unlike Malaysia). No trans-traveler-specific border friction or death in custody is documented (unlike the UAE or Indonesia). But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

Pakistan has a significant hijra/third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in Lahore, and activists are appealing the Shariat Court ruling to the Supreme Court).
records.current_localsOnly: The 2018 Act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the Shariat Court in 2023, under appeal) and the hijra community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented KP violence cases and jirga case-closures describe residents' situation.
records.current_outOfScope: Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: AP (Nov 2024): 'Shooting kills 3 transgender women in Pakistan's largest city' — gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

BBC (21 Sep 2025): police found bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi — latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; article notes estimates of ~500,000 transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief: despite notable legal advances (Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; brief makes custody/police safeguards recommendations.

UK Home Office country-policy note on SOGI, Pakistan, November 2025 (current-status authority): trans/intersex people protected under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 though the Federal Shariat Court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023 leaving ongoing legal disputes; consensual same-sex acts criminalised under PPC s.377 (2 years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male sex), only men criminalised per Human Dignity Trust (Dec 2024); LGBT+ people unlikely to face state persecution.

Amnesty International (19 May 2023): reacting to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 — calls the ruling 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group' of transgender and gender-diverse people; Amnesty had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

The News, Pakistan (21 Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 Rules introduced the neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans Pakistanis still face bullet-riddled bodies on highways, street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion/ridicule at police stations.

Erasing 76crimes (3 Feb 2026, citing the Guardian): a wave of violence has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out — describes the Karachi night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana (three bullets fired through the door, narrowly escaped); also reports Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposing a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

Dawn analysis of the Federal Shariat Court verdict of 19 May 2023 (delivered across 12 shairat petitions): the court ruled sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Transgender Persons Act 2018 (gender identity, right to self-perceived gender identity, inheritance for transgender people) do not conform with petitioners' reading of Islamic principles, and speculated the Act could facilitate rape/sexual assault of women by men 'disguised' as transgender women — framing echoing Western anti-trans moral panic.

The Diplomat (Jul 2025): Pakistan's 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment and healthcare — yet the piece documents citizens 'legally recognized, socially forsaken', i.e. statutory rights not matching lived status.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

records.name: Philippines
records.current_summary:
The Philippines is one of Asia's most socially accepting destinations for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (bakla, tomboy), a vibrant Manila Pride, and no criminalisation. Trans identity has never been criminalised.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (trans people cannot change their gender marker), the SOGIE Equality Bill has been stalled for 25 years (no national anti-discrimination law), and documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a Chinese national arrested for raping a transwoman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The Commission on Human Rights actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction, social acceptance is genuine, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue (documented incidents of bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials).
records.current_localsOnly: The absent LGR law, the 25-year-stalled SOGIE Equality Bill, and the Commission's lack of enforcement power are resident-facing; the 2025 killings affect residents primarily.
records.current_outOfScope: General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Outright/IGLHRC Philippines legal overview (fetched page): lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility updated 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination of clients; openly gay/bisexual people allowed in armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 (uniform policy follows legal gender on birth certificate); Clerical Error Law RA 9048 (2001) blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (judicial order required) and the 2008 Supreme Court ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan bars legal-gender change even after gender-affirming surgery.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): two killings in days — 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist/activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day; Bahaghari says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill, which has been stuck in Congress for 25 years — no national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Manila Bulletin report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (10 Apr 2024): drag artist Taylor Sheesh (Taylor Swift impersonator) was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert on 6 April 2024 — she called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Rolling Stone Philippines explainer (7 Feb 2025): 25 years of legislative inaction on the SOGIE Equality Bill; patchwork protections that do exist — SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur, Iloilo) and 32 cities/municipalities; Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment: P20k-40k fine and/or up to 1 year); Magna Carta of Women and Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic/homophobic/misogynistic slurs and ridicule (fines P1k-10k, up to 30 days, sensitivity seminar).

Rappler: trans Filipinos' legal gender recognition bill would let applicants — including minors with consent — choose markers beyond male/female (X/nonbinary), addressing the lack of a recognition process that drafter Chase Go says drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence; the Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress (28 July).

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel guide (2026 data as of 18 Jun 2026): Manila 'Generally Safe' — LGBTQ+ 69, but Trans travellers only 62 ('Exercise Caution'), HIV+ 81; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions (bakla/tomboy), vibrant Pride/nightlife scene and high media visibility, but SOGIE Bill (filed since 2000) stuck, no marriage equality, Catholic Church resistance; accessibility caveat: 80% of Metro Manila's 46 train stations lack step-free entrances, only 5 of 46 LRT-1 stations have elevators.

HRW report (21 Jun 2017), 'Just Let Us Be': documents bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools, with law short on remedies at the time — basis-level evidence of school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth; includes Tagalog summary and recommendations.

records.name: Vietnam
records.current_summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as "one of Asia's most tolerant countries toward sexual minorities." Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the Civil Code (2015, Article 37) was a landmark that recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented (unlike several neighbours), but conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma, lack of trans-competent providers, and "red tape" in accessing care. In September 2025, Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and five LGBTQ events, shocking activists (though Hanoi's Pride proceeded).

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, and no criminalisation. But Vietnam is a one-party authoritarian state where "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice" (Amnesty), and the stalled LGR means no practical gender-marker change. The UN Development Programme is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.
records.current_localsOnly: The stalled Gender Affirmation Law, the SOGICE conversion efforts, and the healthcare discrimination barriers are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: One-party state political controls, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

Lighthouse Vietnam study (Oct 2024): 'Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam' - documents experiences and forms of SOGICE in the Vietnamese context, with comprehensive data needs analysis.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House 3 Mar 2021); multi-source treatment briefing covering society/authorities in Hanoi and HCMC across education, employment, housing, health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

records.name: Peru
records.current_summary:
Peru demands real caution with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence against trans people, but no criminalisation of trans identity and an unprecedented 17-year conviction for police torture of a trans woman. Congress approved (February-April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated axis-C restriction comparable to US state bans or the UK EHRC code. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 TLGBI people were assassinated (trans women most affected). In the Azul Rojas Marín case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025) — an unprecedented conviction for Peru and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. A presidential decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024), but was walked back after massive protests.

For a visitor: no border friction, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure when using public facilities.
records.current_localsOnly: The court-based LGR process (expensive, years-long, no self-ID law) is resident-facing; the 54 assassinations and the Azul Rojas Marín torture case concern residents.
records.current_outOfScope: General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's committee approved unanimously (for plenary) the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 (presented by Jorge Montoya and Honor y Democracia party) that threatens trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis: the bathroom-restriction article openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights; also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024): report finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho (trans human-rights defender/journalist) stresses recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; cites the 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

BBC News Mundo (19 Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, trans woman and LGBTI activist — Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history (case reached the Court via the CIDH).

Infobae Peru (15 Dec 2025): officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León sentenced to 17 years for the rape/torture of Azul Rojas — the sentence landing nearly 20 years after the attack; judgment issued by the judiciary after years of litigation.

HRW (19 May 2025): the April-2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people — including trans youth — from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles (art.4 media/advertising ban, art.5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content; obscenity-minimum sentence raised 3→4 years; HRW says child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating.

HRW dispatch (27 Jun 2024): Peru's health system walked back anti-trans guidance — authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity' for trans patients in healthcare settings.

Outright International current Peru overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; April 2025's 'sexual integrity' law restricts restrooms by biological sex; April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order/security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually since 2002 (oldest recorded 1984).

Peru Support Group (Apr 2025): week-in-review of setbacks — Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR (Muñante/Montoya) banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; Willax TV's Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed first openly-lesbian congresswoman Susel Paredes ('go use the men's room'); congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at INMP.

The Perchy Bird: Peru's Congress voted to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions — Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carried the repeal (arguing the President lacked authority to issue the anti-discrimination decree), after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a claimed 1M-signature removal petition; the piece notes the outcome made Peru one of only three South American countries (with Paraguay and Guyana) lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

records.name: Qatar
records.current_summary:
Qatar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf. Human Rights Watch interviewed four transgender women arrested by the Preventive Security Department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Arrests continued even during the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.
records.current_outOfScope: Migrant-worker abuses, kafala labour system, and general human-rights concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

sources.claim: HRW (24 Oct 2022): security forces arrested and abused LGBT people - six cases of severe repeated beatings and five sexual harassment cases in police custody 2019-2022, arrests in public places based solely on gender expression and unlawful searches; mistreatment as recent as September 2022 as Qatar prepared to host the 2022 World Cup under global scrutiny.

Wikipedia LGBTQ rights in Qatar: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years for Muslims and non-Muslims; Sharia allows a capital sentence never imposed); documented beatings/torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Baseline legal-persecution picture.

PinkNews (20 Jul 2018): taboo around homosexuality - Doha News' 2016 piece by a gay Qatari ('jarring', 'irreparable damage to mental health') drew extreme reactions; Swansea University lecturer on World Cup conduct; pre-tournament climate report. Social-climate evidence, no legal change.

records.name: Bahrain
records.current_summary:
Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare."

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment.
records.current_outOfScope: Political repression, restrictions on free expression, and labour concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

sources.claim: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. For this record: tertiary overview consistent with the Outright/State Department baseline — orientation source only, not stand-alone evidence.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade — including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International — so local media often serve as the only source. For this record: an evidence-reliability caveat — most findings for this jurisdiction rest on thin, partly remote sourcing.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy — but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people (the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation). For this record: decriminalisation with the residual-arrest pattern — the nuance a visitor's safety turns on.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011–Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. For this record: a SOURCE CONFLICT — this contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia/Outright/2023 US State Dept; treat as unresolved, flagged for intake follow-up rather than ground truth.

freshness_all.fact: Consensual same-sex conduct not criminalised (2023 US State); courts since 2023 reject gender-affirming procedures; legal gender recognition still denied.

records.name: Oman
records.current_summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — and uniquely in the Gulf, combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveler abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the Royal Oman Police publicly announced arresting transgender women in Salalah after private-party photos circulated on social media; HRW documented arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travelers: in February 2024, Nin Kala, an Indian non-binary model and designer arriving at Muscat airport on a tourist visa, was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. Kala warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these Gulf countries."
records.current_outOfScope: Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Oman's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Cairo 52 + White Tent joint stakeholder submission (6 Aug 2025) to Oman's 4th-cycle UN UPR: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression, says Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, and reports Oman ignores earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access; recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.

Statute-level extraction from Oman's Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018): Art 265 public indecency (10 days-3 months + OMR 100-300 fine), Art 266 impersonating/entering women-only venues disguised (1 month-1 year), Arts 267-268 producing or sharing content 'violating public morals' offline and online (up to 1 year / 10 days-1 month), plus Cyber Crime Law 2011 Arts 17/31 used against LGBT expression (1 month-3 years + OMR 100-3000); gender non-conformity punished through Art 266(d).

LegalClarity overview (published 3 Jun 2026): Oman criminalises all same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' prison under the 2018 Penal Code, prosecution often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations without a family complaint (Art 49 dual-criminality exception); Art 60 requires deportation for foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent) and allows it for misdemeanours (3-15 years); state ISP Omantel enables surveillance; outing carries social AND criminal risk; assembly/advocacy restricted via the Civil Associations Law.

Visitor-facing incident (27 Feb 2023): a genderqueer/non-binary Indian model-activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — direct first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

HRW open letter (13 Jul 2020) to Oman's authorities on arrests/convictions under the 2018 Penal Code's 'imitating the opposite sex' provision: Royal Oman Police announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after Snapchat photos from a private Salalah party circulated, and an Asian expat in abaya/niqab at an Al Buraimi women-only park hour — shows active enforcement of the cross-dressing offence against gender non-conformity.

HRW regional report (16 Apr 2018) with MENA laws annex covering Oman: documents that Oman's 2018 penal code (effective that year) added a retrograde provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside regional comparison (Kuwait's 2007 imitation law), and records Oman's existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012): distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons; in some Islamic countries acts are criminalised (even by death) while identity alone is not - scholarly context for Oman's legal-religious framework.

records.name: Slovakia
records.current_summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, EU free movement, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside Tepláreň, a Bratislava LGBT bar — classified as Slovakia's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: parliament advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in Bratislava.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition.
records.current_localsOnly: The 40-year-old medicalised LGR regime and the LGR-ban bill are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: The LGR-ban bill and constitutional gender amendments are resident-facing climate signals. Roma discrimination is out of scope.

sources.claim: Wikipedia timeline of the 12 October 2022 Bratislava shooting: a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger (the LGBT bar Teplaren was 'plan B') arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at Teplaren, killing two and injuring one. The article's investigation, victims and perpetrator sections document the planning, the LGBT-venue target and the aftermath.

Feature of 7 February 2023: Slovakia's trans community remains precarious after the 12 October 2022 terrorist attack on the Bratislava LGBT bar, which rights groups say 'marked a new era' for trans people in the country. Existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought even greater fears about the future.
thin: no usable finding

Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović's letter (April 2023) to the Slovak National Council: six months after the Tepláreň attack, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the LGR ban bill.
thin: no usable finding
